99.title: The Jesus Prayer
99.hook: Orthodox Christians repeat Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me, with the breath
99.howItsDone: Orthodox Christians pray the Jesus Prayer, 'Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me', often many times a day, sometimes with a prayer rope and in rhythm with the breath. Many Catholic, Anglican and Protestant Christians use it too.

segments.voice: Yesterday, ACTS: adoration, confession, thanksgiving, supplication. Your line was a shape helps. Did you get from A to S? Day ninety-nine.

Paul tells one of his churches, in the King James Bible: "Pray without ceasing." Three words. And if you've ever tried to take them literally, you know the problem. You have a job. You have dishes. You have to sleep. How could anyone pray all the time? There's an old Russian book, written down in the 1800s by an unknown author, called The Way of a Pilgrim. It tells of a wanderer who hears those three words read in church and can't stop thinking about them. He walks from town to town, asking priests and monks how it's done. Most give him sermons. Finally an old monk gives him something much smaller: one sentence, to say over and over, until it begins to say itself.
screen: `PRAY WITHOUT CEASING.` → `A WANDERER ASKS HOW.` → `ONE SENTENCE.`

segments.voice: The sentence is the Jesus Prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me. Many add at the end: a sinner. It's a very short prayer with very old roots. On the road out of Jericho, a blind beggar named Bartimaeus hears Jesus passing and shouts, in the King James: "Jesus, thou son of David, have mercy on me." People tell him to be quiet; he shouts louder. And in Jesus's story of two men praying in the temple, the tax collector can't even look up; he just says, "God be merciful to me a sinner." Put those two cries together and you have the Jesus Prayer. By the fourth and fifth centuries, monks in the Egyptian desert were repeating short prayers like this all day long while they worked, and over centuries the practice was treasured especially in the Orthodox churches, in the monasteries of Mount Athos in Greece, and in Russia. The tradition is sometimes called hesychasm, from the Greek for stillness. Many who pray it use a prayer rope, a loop of woven knots, moving one knot for each prayer. And many join it to the breath: breathing in, Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God; breathing out, have mercy on me. What does mercy mean here? Not just let me off. The Greek word eleos is the same one sung in the old church cry, Kyrie eleison, Lord have mercy, and it carries a sense of compassion, of kindness poured out. Western Christians, Catholic, Anglican and Protestant, have taken up the Jesus Prayer too. The pilgrim in the old story says that after a while, the prayer started praying in him, even while he walked.
screen: `BARTIMAEUS SHOUTS LOUDER.` · `GOD BE MERCIFUL TO ME.` · `DESERT, ATHOS, RUSSIA.` · `WITH THE BREATH, ON A ROPE.` · then, large: `HAVE MERCY ON ME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: ten times, slowly, with your breath. Sit comfortably, and let your breathing find its own pace. If you pray, try the Jesus Prayer. Breathing in: Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God. Breathing out: have mercy on me. Count on your fingers if it helps. Don't rush, and don't worry when your mind wanders; just come back to the words. If you don't pray, you can simply breathe, and listen to the words as someone else's prayer, or rest on a single word, like mercy. The bell holds the time.
The Jesus Prayer. Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me: a blind man's shout and a tax collector's whisper, said with the breath.

Your line: have mercy on me. Today, at one hard moment, breathe in, breathe out, and let those words, or just the word mercy, go with the breath. Tomorrow, day one hundred, and the most famous psalm. Day ninety-nine.

100.title: Praying the Psalms (Psalm 23)
100.hook: for three thousand years people have prayed with borrowed words
100.howItsDone: Christians pray and sing the Psalms in worship every week, and monks and many others pray them daily; the Rule of Saint Benedict covers all 150 in a week, and the Book of Common Prayer in a month. Psalm 23 is read at many Christian funerals.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Jesus Prayer, said with the breath. Your line was have mercy on me. Did the words go with you into a hard moment? And today: one hundred days. Day one hundred.

Think of the times you didn't have words of your own. At a funeral. In the middle of the night after bad news. On a day so good you wanted to shout but didn't know what to shout. What people often reach for, in those moments, are borrowed words. A song. A poem. A line someone else wrote, that says it better than you could. At funerals in many countries, even people who never go to church often find they know one set of words by heart. The Lord is my shepherd; I shall not want. Those words come from a book of a hundred and fifty prayers and songs, which people have been praying, in one form or another, for close to three thousand years. It's the prayer book inside the Bible.
screen: `WHEN YOU HAVE NO WORDS.` → `BORROWED WORDS.` → `THE PRAYER BOOK INSIDE THE BIBLE.`

segments.voice: Today's word is psalter, the name for the book of Psalms, especially when it's used for praying. It comes from the Greek for a stringed instrument, because these were songs. The Hebrew name is Tehillim: praises. Tradition links many of them to King David, the shepherd boy who became king around three thousand years ago, though many were written by others, over centuries. And here's what surprises people: they're not all praise. There's joy, but also rage, fear, loneliness, and complaints that sound almost rude. They give you words for every mood. Jesus prayed them. On the cross, his cry, my God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me, is the first line of Psalm twenty-two. Jews have prayed the psalms every day for many centuries, and still do. Christian monks, following the Rule of Saint Benedict, pray all one hundred and fifty every week, and the Anglican prayer book walks through them every month. Now listen to the most famous one. In the King James Bible: "The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want. He maketh me to lie down in green pastures: he leadeth me beside the still waters." Where the King James prints LORD in capital letters, the Hebrew has God's own personal name, which Jews, out of reverence, do not say aloud. And the psalm doesn't pretend life is easy: "Yea, though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil: for thou art with me; thy rod and thy staff they comfort me." Notice the turn. The first lines talk about God. Then, in the dark valley, it starts talking to him: thou art with me. That's what praying with borrowed words can do. You start by reading. You end up talking.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read Psalm twenty-three aloud, slowly. If you have a Bible or a phone nearby, find it; it's only six verses. Read it out loud, at half your normal speed, pausing at every comma. If you don't have it, say the lines you heard today: the Lord is my shepherd; I shall not want. Notice which phrase catches, and stay with it. If you pray, let the psalm be your prayer. If you don't, let it be a poem that thousands of people have leaned on. The bell holds the time.

Your line: the lord is my shepherd. Today, when you're short of words, borrow these. Tomorrow, an old monastic way of reading a few words slowly. Day one hundred.

101.title: Lectio divina
101.hook: an old monastic way: read a short passage, notice a word, ponder it, rest
101.howItsDone: Monks and nuns practice lectio divina daily, and many Catholic, Anglican, Orthodox and Protestant Christians use it alone or in small groups, reading a short passage slowly several times, sharing a word that stood out, praying, and resting in silence.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the psalter, the prayer book inside the Bible. Your line was the lord is my shepherd. When did you borrow those words? Day one hundred and one.

How do you read now? Probably fast. Scrolling, skimming, headlines, the first two lines of a message and then the next one. Most of us read like we're looking for something and we're late. Now picture a monastery in the Middle Ages. A monk sits with a book, and he reads a single sentence aloud, quietly, to himself. Then he reads it again. And again. He isn't trying to finish. He isn't trying to learn a fact for a test. He's trying to taste it. The monks had a word for this, taken from the way a cow chews the same mouthful over and over, slowly, all afternoon. They called it rumination. And they had a name for the whole practice. It means sacred reading.
screen: `SCROLLING, SKIMMING, LATE.` → `ONE SENTENCE, AGAIN AND AGAIN.` → `CHEWING IT SLOWLY.`

segments.voice: Lectio divina is Latin: divine reading, sacred reading. Saint Benedict, who wrote a rule for monks in the sixth century, set aside hours every day for it. And in the twelfth century a monk named Guigo, the head of a Carthusian monastery in the French Alps, described it as a ladder with four rungs. The first is lectio, reading. You read a short passage slowly, often aloud, and notice which word or phrase catches you. The second is meditatio, pondering. You turn that word over, chew it, ask what it's saying to you today. The third is oratio, prayer: you answer God, in your own words, about what you've noticed. And the fourth is contemplatio, contemplation, which is the hardest to explain because it isn't really doing anything. You rest. You stop talking and simply stay, the way you'd sit with someone you love without needing to speak. Guigo put it in a picture: reading puts the food in your mouth, pondering chews it, prayer tastes it, and contemplation is the sweetness itself. The point isn't to cover much. A whole morning might be spent on one line. That's hard for us. We want to get through it. But lectio divina says the opposite: go slowly enough and one word is enough. For centuries it lived mostly in monasteries. Today Catholics, Anglicans, Orthodox and many Protestants use it, alone or in small groups, where people read a passage aloud three or four times and each shares the one word that stayed with them. It works best with a short passage. A single verse from the Psalms is plenty. Try this one: "Be still, and know that I am God."
screen: `DIVINE READING.` · `A LADDER WITH FOUR RUNGS.` · `READ, PONDER, PRAY, REST.` · `FOOD, CHEWING, TASTE, SWEETNESS.` · then, large: `ONE WORD IS ENOUGH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read one verse four times. Use the one you just heard: be still, and know that I am God. First, just say it slowly, and notice which word catches you. Maybe still. Maybe know. Second, say it again, and turn that one word over. Third, if you pray, say it once more and answer God about it; if you don't, answer yourself. Fourth, say it one last time, and then rest in the quiet without doing anything at all. The bell holds the time.
Lectio divina. Latin for sacred reading: read, ponder, pray, rest, with a very few words.
Your line: one word is enough. Today, carry the word that caught you, and come back to it three times before bed. Tomorrow, a nightly look back at the day. Day one hundred and one.

102.title: The examen
102.hook: Ignatius taught a nightly look back: where was God today, where did I miss him?
102.howItsDone: Jesuits and many other Catholics pray the examen once or twice daily, often at night, and many Anglicans and Protestants use it too: giving thanks, asking for light, reviewing the day, asking forgiveness, and looking ahead to tomorrow.

segments.voice: Yesterday, lectio divina: read, ponder, pray, rest. Your line was one word is enough. Which word stayed with you? Day one hundred and two.

It's late. You're lying in bed, and your mind does the thing it does: it replays the day. Usually the worst bits. The awkward thing you said. The email you shouldn't have sent. Round and round. Now go to Spain, 1521. A young Basque soldier named Iñigo, proud, vain, in love with glory, has his leg smashed by a cannonball defending a fortress. For months he lies in bed recovering. He asks for adventure novels. There aren't any in the house. All they have is a life of Christ and a book of saints' stories. So, bored, he reads those. And he starts to notice something odd about his own daydreams. That noticing will turn into a prayer practiced around the world.
screen: `REPLAYING THE DAY.` → `A SOLDIER, A CANNONBALL.` → `NOTICING HIS DAYDREAMS.`

segments.voice: Here's what he noticed. When he daydreamed about winning glory and impressing a great lady, it was exciting at the time, but afterward he felt dry and empty. When he daydreamed about living like the saints, the good feeling stayed. He began to believe God was speaking through those after-feelings. The soldier became Ignatius of Loyola, founder of the Jesuits, and he wrote a manual for prayer called the Spiritual Exercises. In it is a short daily practice called the examen, from the Latin for weighing, like the needle on a scale. It's a look back over the day, and it has five steps. First, give thanks, for the specific gifts of today. Second, ask for light, to see the day honestly. Third, walk back through the day, hour by hour, and notice: where was God in it? Where did I feel alive, close, grateful? And where did I miss him, turn away, feel empty? Fourth, ask forgiveness for what needs it. Fifth, look ahead to tomorrow with hope. Notice where it starts. Not with what you did wrong. With thanks. It isn't the bedtime replay of your worst moments. It's a search for God in the ordinary hours, like the old prayer in the Psalms: "Search me, O God, and know my heart: try me, and know my thoughts." The Jesuits have long told the story that Ignatius said his companions could skip other prayers on a busy day, but never the examen. It's not only for Jesuits. Catholics, Anglicans and many Protestants pray it too, usually at night, in about the time it takes to brush your teeth. And its whole question fits in five words: where was he today?
screen: `DRY, OR CONSOLED?` · `EXAMEN: A WEIGHING.` · `THANKS, LIGHT, REVIEW.` · `SORRY, THEN HOPE.` · then, large: `WHERE WAS HE TODAY?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: review today in two minutes. Sit, and breathe. First, name one specific thing from today you're thankful for. Then, if you pray, ask God to help you see honestly. Now rewind the day like a film, from waking until now. Don't judge it. Just notice. Where did you feel most alive? Where did you feel far away, or small? Stop on one moment of each. If you pray, you can say sorry for what needs it, and ask for help tomorrow. If you don't, just note what you've learned. The bell holds the time.
Examen. From the Latin for weighing. Ignatius's nightly look back: thanks, light, review, sorry, and hope for tomorrow.
Your line: where was he today? Tonight, before you sleep, let the replay be the examen: start with thanks. Tomorrow, prayers that take three seconds. Day one hundred and two.

103.title: Arrow prayers (Nehemiah 2:4)
103.hook: before the king answers, Nehemiah fires a silent prayer upward
103.howItsDone: Many Christians pray short, silent prayers through the day, before a meeting, at a siren, in a moment of fear, alongside longer times of prayer; Orthodox Christians often use the Jesus Prayer this way.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the examen: Ignatius's nightly look back over the day. Your line was where was he today? Did you find a moment, or a miss? Today, a prayer that takes about one second. Day one hundred three.

You know the moment. Someone important turns to you and says, so, what do you want? The interview. The doctor. The boss with one minute between meetings. Your mouth is open, and there's no time to think. Now go to the Persian court, about four and a half centuries before Jesus. A Jewish man named Nehemiah is cupbearer to King Artaxerxes: he pours the king's wine and tastes it first. He's just heard that the walls of Jerusalem are rubble, and he can't hide his grief. The king notices his sad face, and the text says, "Then I was very sore afraid." A sad servant in front of a king was a risk. And then the king asks the question. What do you want? Nehemiah has maybe a second. Today is what he does with it.
screen: `WHAT DO YOU WANT?` → `A CUPBEARER TO A KING.` → `ONE SECOND TO ANSWER.`

segments.voice: Here's the verse, in the King James Bible: "Then the king said unto me, For what dost thou make request? So I prayed to the God of heaven." And in the very next breath, he answers the king. That's it. No words recorded, no kneeling, no closed eyes. Between the question and the answer, a prayer went up, and nobody in the room saw it. Christians came to call this kind of prayer an arrow prayer: short, silent, fired upward in the middle of life. Old writers told of monks in the Egyptian desert who prayed this way all day, in quick, brief bursts. But notice something about Nehemiah. The arrow didn't come from nowhere. In chapter one, when the bad news first came, he sat down and wept, and fasted and prayed for days. Months passed before the king ever asked. So the arrow flew from a bow that had been strung for a long time. The long prayer and the short one belong together. The Bible is full of these arrows. A mother pleading for her daughter, in Matthew: "Lord, help me." Peter, sinking into the waves: "Lord, save me." Three words each. And Paul tells the church in Thessalonica, "Pray without ceasing," which many Christians hear not as a command to never stop talking, but as an invitation to keep a door open all day. Catholics, Orthodox Christians and Protestants all have their short prayers for the middle of things. For Nehemiah, it worked: the king said yes, and he went home to rebuild the wall.
screen: `A PRAYER BETWEEN QUESTION AND ANSWER.` · `THE BOW WAS STRUNG FOR MONTHS.` · `LORD, HELP ME. LORD, SAVE ME.` · then, large: `PRAY WITHOUT CEASING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: rehearse the arrow. Settle, and breathe. Think of the next conversation you'll have today. Who is it with? A coworker, a child, a cashier, someone on the phone. Picture their face. Now, before the first word, take three seconds. If you pray, you can send up a short line, like the mother's, "Lord, help me," or a few words of your own. If you don't, take one slow breath and wish them well. Then let the rest of the time be quiet. When that conversation actually comes, do it for real. Three seconds. The bell holds the time.
Arrow prayers. Short, silent prayers sent up in the middle of life, like Nehemiah's before the king. Today's word.
Your line: short prayers fly. Today, before your next hard conversation, take three seconds first. Nobody has to know. Day one hundred three.

104.title: Praying for others by name
104.hook: Christians pray for people by name, trusting God hears
104.howItsDone: Christians pray for others by name in private prayer and in church: the prayers of the people in many liturgies, the reading of names in Orthodox services, and prayer lists and prayer chains in many Protestant churches.

segments.voice: Yesterday, arrow prayers: Nehemiah's one-second prayer before the king. Your line was short prayers fly. Did you take three seconds before a conversation? Day one hundred four.

Somebody texts you: please pray for my dad, surgery Thursday. Maybe you pray. Maybe you don't know what to do with that message. Either way, it's one of the oldest requests people make. Here's an old picture of it, from Exodus. Israel is in a battle, and Moses stands on a hill above it with his arms raised. The story says that while his hands were up, Israel prevailed, and when they dropped, Israel lost ground. But arms get heavy. So two men, his brother Aaron and a man named Hur, sit Moses on a stone, and stand on either side, and hold his arms up for him until sunset. In the King James words, "Aaron and Hur stayed up his hands." Christians have long read that picture as prayer for someone else. Today's word is its name.
screen: `PLEASE PRAY FOR MY DAD.` → `ARMS ON A HILL.` → `AARON AND HUR HOLD THEM UP.`

segments.voice: Intercession. It comes from Latin, to go between. To intercede is to step in on someone's behalf, to stand between them and what they're facing, and bring them before God. The New Testament puts it on the list early. Paul writes to Timothy: "I exhort therefore, that, first of all, supplications, prayers, intercessions, and giving of thanks, be made for all men." First of all. For all people. And the Bible is full of people praying for others. Abraham bargains with God over a whole city. Jesus tells Peter, before Peter's worst night, that he has prayed for him, that his faith would not fail. On the cross, Jesus prays for the soldiers: "Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do." Now notice the names. Paul's letters are crowded with them: people he remembers when he prays, one by one. A name makes it real. Not the sick in general. Marta, in room four. Churches do this in different ways. In Catholic, Anglican and Lutheran services, the prayers of the people bring the sick, the grieving and the world before God. In Orthodox liturgy, the priest reads out names of the living and the departed. Many evangelical churches run prayer chains, a phone tree of people praying for whoever needs it this week. Catholics and Orthodox Christians also ask Mary and the saints to pray for them, the way you'd ask a friend; many Protestants ask only God, and their friends still on earth. What they share is James's plain instruction: "pray one for another." Nobody claims to know exactly how it works. Christians say God hears, and that holding someone up changes something, often in the one who holds.
screen: `INTERCESSION: TO GO BETWEEN.` · `FIRST OF ALL, FOR ALL PEOPLE.` · `A NAME MAKES IT REAL.` · `EVERY CHURCH HOLDS PEOPLE UP.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name three people. Settle, and breathe. Let the first name come: someone who's struggling right now. Say it, quietly or in your head. Picture their face. If you pray, hold them up to God, in a sentence or in silence. If you don't, hold them in your attention and wish them well. Stay there for a few breaths. Then a second name: someone you love and don't worry about. Then a third: someone difficult. That one's harder. Just their name is enough. The bell holds the time.
Intercession. From Latin, to go between. Praying for someone else, by name, bringing them before God. Today's word.
Your line: hold them up. Today, when someone tells you what they're carrying, remember their name tonight, and hold them up, the way you can. Day one hundred four.

105.title: How long, O Lord? (Psalm 13)
105.hook: the Bible gives you permission to complain to God
105.howItsDone: Christians pray the lament psalms in daily prayer, at funerals and in times of crisis, and many churches hold services of lament after tragedies; some people write their own complaints to God in a journal, following the psalms' shape.

segments.voice: Yesterday, intercession, and your line: hold them up. Whose name did you carry? This week, ways to pray: the Jesus Prayer, the Psalms, lectio divina, the examen, arrows, names. Today, the one people are surprised is allowed. Day one hundred five.

It's two in the morning. The diagnosis hasn't changed. The job still hasn't come through. The person still hasn't called back. You've been polite about it for months. And somewhere inside, a very impolite question is building. Many people assume there are two options here: swallow it, or walk away from God entirely. The Bible offers a third, and it's in the middle of its own prayer book. A psalm that opens with a complaint, and doesn't apologize for it. In the King James words: "How long wilt thou forget me, O LORD? for ever? how long wilt thou hide thy face from me?" That's not a whisper. That's somebody at the end of their rope, talking straight to God. Today's word is what this kind of prayer is called.
screen: `TWO IN THE MORNING.` → `SWALLOW IT, OR WALK AWAY?` → `A THIRD WAY: HOW LONG?`

segments.voice: Lament. A prayer of grief and complaint, spoken to God. You met this psalm back on day sixteen, with David shouting at God. Today, look at how a lament is built, because the shape is the teaching. The first two verses ask how long, four times. Then the psalm asks for something: "Consider and hear me, O LORD my God: lighten mine eyes." Look at me. Answer me. And then it turns: "But I have trusted in thy mercy; my heart shall rejoice in thy salvation." Complaint, request, trust. Notice what hasn't changed. Nothing outside. No answer arrives between verse four and verse five. The turn happens in the one praying. Scholars count around a third of the Psalms as laments, and some aren't one person's cry but a whole people's, after a defeat or a famine. Not all of them turn; Psalm 88 never does. Then there's a whole book of lament. Lamentations grieves Jerusalem after the Babylonians burned it. And look at how it's made. Four of its five chapters are acrostics: each verse starts with the next letter of the Hebrew alphabet. Grief, set out from A to Z. Some readers hear in that a way of saying all of it, every letter, and of giving pain a shape with an end. Here's the idea under all of it. You don't complain to someone you think isn't there. A lament keeps talking to God while saying, this hurts, and it isn't right. Jews have prayed these psalms for many centuries, and on Tisha B'Av, the fast that mourns the temple, Lamentations is chanted aloud. Christians of every church pray the laments too. For both, honesty isn't the opposite of faith. Sometimes it's what faith sounds like at two in the morning.
screen: `HOW LONG? FOUR TIMES.` · `COMPLAINT, REQUEST, TRUST.` · `GRIEF FROM A TO Z.` · then, large: `YOU DON'T COMPLAIN TO NOBODY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: write one honest complaint. Get something to write on, or open a note on your phone. Settle, and breathe. What's the thing you've been polite about for too long? Write it in one or two sentences, plainly. If you pray, you can start it the way the psalm does: how long. If you don't pray, write it to whoever or whatever you'd want to hear it. Don't tidy it up. Don't add a happy ending unless one comes. Then put the pen down and sit with it. The bell holds the time.
Lament. A prayer of grief and complaint, spoken to God rather than about him. Around a third of the Psalms are laments. Today's word.
Your line: complaint is a prayer too. Today, keep what you wrote. Read it once more tonight, and notice whether anything has shifted, even a little. Fifteen weeks on the path. Day one hundred five.
